title: Fossanova (1274)
hookLine: he dies on the way to a council, aged about forty-nine

cards: A letter arrives from the pope, the early accounts say. There's to be a great council of the Church in Lyon, in France, and Thomas is wanted there.

So the man who has stopped writing gets on the road anyway, heading north from Naples with his companions. Somewhere along the way he falls ill and can't go on. The door that finally opens to him isn't a Dominican house.
It belongs to white-robed Cistercian monks, in an abbey called Fossanova.

teach.b: Tradition tells the last days quietly. The monks of Fossanova take him in. He's a stranger, a friar, not one of their own, and they nurse him anyway.

teach.h: THE SONG OF SONGS AT THE END.
teach.b: Sick as he was, tradition says, he spoke to them about the Song of Songs, the love poem in the middle of the Bible. The great arguer, at the end, talking about love.
At his last Communion, the early accounts give him words of deep faith in Christ present in the sacrament, the same faith as the Corpus Christi hymns tradition credits to him.
Then he dies there, among Cistercians, far from Paris and the lecture halls, his great book unfinished.

teach.h: A COURSE FINISHED, A BOOK NOT.
teach.b: Paul, near his own end, says in the Douay-Rheims: "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith." Thomas didn't finish his Summa. Catholics would say he finished his course.
After his death the Church named him a saint, and later a Doctor of the Church, a teacher for the whole Church.
And Catholics gave him a nickname that stuck: the Angelic Doctor. People explain it in different ways. Some point to his careful writing on the angels.
Others point to his life, which his companions remembered as pure and gentle, almost unearthly in its calm. Both reasons are told; neither is the whole of it.
One more quiet detail: the friar who gave his life to teaching was cared for at the end by monks of a praying order.

how: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Thomas Aquinas, the Angelic Doctor, with Mass and sometimes with prayers for students and teachers, and some Catholic schools and universities honor him as a patron.

games.q: you're Thomas. you've stopped writing, but the pope asks you to come to a council far away. what do you do?
o: set out on the road anyway.
games.why: he sets out, falls ill on the way, and is taken in by the Cistercian monks of Fossanova, where he dies.

practice: Bring to mind someone who studies or teaches: a professor, a teacher you had in school, a student up too late, someone writing a book nobody may read, and picture their desk, their tired eyes.
If you pray, ask God to give them light, and rest when their work runs out; if you don't, hold them in mind with thanks for what they've handed on.

wordCard.voice: Fossanova. The Cistercian abbey where Thomas, on his way to a council, fell ill, was cared for by monks, and died. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: the Angelic Doctor, the title Catholics gave Thomas.
